figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), a simple noise-modulation method for motion-controllable diffusion video generation. (a) Prior methods rely on spatial noise warping driven by motion fields. They preserve spatial Gaussianity only through costly correction steps. (b) HME instead applies per-location Householder transformations in channel space to the noise. It preserves spatial Gaussianity by construction, with a $2.7\times$ speed-up and better motion adherence. HME naturally supports (c1) motion transfer, (c2) local object motion control, and (c3) camera motion control.

abstract: Diffusion models for video generation have achieved remarkable success, yet precise motion control under explicit user guidance remains challenging. Recent noise-warping methods introduce temporal correlations by warping the noise according to the user-provided motion signal. However, standard spatial warping generally disrupts the noise’s i.i.d. Gaussian structure, requiring distribution correction, such as Jacobian-based correction, but at a substantial computational overhead. We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), which encodes the motion signal into the noise through a sequence of Householder reflections that together form an orthogonal transformation applied to each location’s channel vector. HME exactly preserves the spatial Gaussian structure within each frame while introducing cross-frame correlations that promote temporally consistent video. HME is agnostic to the network architecture and integrates directly into standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines. Experiments on different scenarios show that HME matches or outperforms the state of the art, while achieving a 2.7× speedup over noise warping. These results demonstrate that per-location Householder transformations in channel space offer a principled and efficient alternative to noise warping for motion-controllable video generation.

sections.body: The paper argues that spatial noise warping breaks the i.i.d. Gaussian structure of diffusion noise and therefore needs correction. HME instead applies per-location orthogonal transformations in channel space, built as products of Householder reflections, to the noise at initialization. Because the transform is orthogonal, each frame's noise stays exactly Gaussian by construction, and no Jacobian correction is needed. The method requires no changes to the architecture or loss and accepts any dense optical flow. The authors report a 2.7× speedup in noise processing time and improved motion adherence on three benchmarks, and they demonstrate the method on CogVideoX. The stated contributions also include a derivation of the cross-frame covariance.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Householder Motion Embedding replaces spatial noise warping with per-location orthogonal transforms, avoiding Gaussianity correction.

sections.body: Motion-control methods are grouped into local object control, global camera control and motion transfer, and most inject motion after the noise is drawn. Noise-warping methods instead transport the initial noise along optical flow: PYoCo introduced correlated noise across frames, HIWYN added integral noise, InfRes used Brownian bridge increments, and GWTF provided a linear-time warping algorithm. The paper states that these methods share one limitation: spatial resampling disrupts the i.i.d. Gaussian structure, which needs costly post-hoc correction at higher resolutions. HME is positioned as replacing spatial transport with per-location orthogonal transformations that preserve Gaussianity exactly. Householder transformations have prior uses in position encoding and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: All existing noise-warping methods disturb Gaussian noise structure via spatial resampling, requiring costly correction.

sections.body: A Householder reflector is an orthogonal matrix defined by one non-zero vector, and any orthogonal matrix decomposes into at most C reflections. Optical flow is resampled to the latent grid, and fixed random projections `A_k` and `b_k` lift each two-dimensional flow vector into K reflection vectors in the C-dimensional channel space. Each frame's noise is the previous frame's noise multiplied by the product of the K reflections at that location. Proposition 1 states that, because the product is orthogonal, each frame remains marginally standard Gaussian and locations stay independent. The projections total 3KC values and are not learned. The cross-frame covariance is an orthogonal matrix determined by the local flow.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Flow-conditioned products of Householder reflections build noise that stays exactly Gaussian in every frame.

sections.body: The base model is the pretrained CogVideoX-5B-I2V, fine-tuned on 100K videos from RealCam-Vid for 30,000 iterations with a rank-2048 LoRA setup. On motion transfer over 45 videos, all three variants (γ ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}) beat six baselines on all ten metrics. At γ=0.5, flow error falls from 5.644 (GWTF) to 4.486, and PSNR rises from 14.748 to 15.162 dB relative to GWTF. On MC-Bench, the method beats GWTF on five metrics, with lower CTD (13.879 vs 15.747), but GWTF is higher on Bg-Obj CTD (42.44 against 39.53). At K=2, runtime is 2.80 ms per latent, against 7.63 ms for GWTF.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On the motion-transfer benchmark, all three variants beat six baselines on all ten metrics, with flow error 4.486 against the noise-warping baseline's 5.644.

sections.body: The discussion compares per-location encoding with GWTF's transport. The noise at each location keeps its norm, and its change between frames depends only on the local flow. Regions with the same motion receive the same transform, and static regions also change when the bias is non-zero. The authors hypothesise that this direct channel-space conditioning explains the motion-adherence gain over GWTF. The stated limitations are the expressivity-efficiency trade-off in K, reliance on accurate optical flow for training, and difficulty with complex non-rigid motion such as the snowboarder in the DAVIS examples. The section also notes that fine-tuning is still required and that baselines were evaluated with released checkpoints rather than retrained.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Limitations include dependence on accurate optical flow, difficulty with non-rigid motion, and the need for fine-tuning.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the method: per-location Householder transformations in latent channel space replace spatial noise transport, keep spatial Gaussianity by construction, and encode motion-aligned temporal correlations. The authors report that experiments on motion transfer, object-level control and camera control show improved motion adherence, visual fidelity and noise-processing efficiency over existing noise-warping methods. They suggest that geometric transformation-based conditioning may offer a way to add structured motion priors to video diffusion models beyond noise construction. The section introduces no new results or numbers.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Per-location Householder transforms improve motion adherence, fidelity and noise-processing efficiency over noise-warping methods.

sections.body: The appendix contains extended related work on image-to-video models and Householder applications, preliminaries on latent video diffusion, and fine-tuning details. It also gives the evaluation protocol for DAVIS, MC-Bench and DL3DV, the proof of Proposition 1, and the cross-frame covariance derivation. In the Gaussianity tests, HME's Moran's I p-values range from 0.466 to 0.534, interpolation-based operations give Moran's I p-values of 0.008–0.020, and nearest-neighbor sampling gives a K-S p-value of 0.115. The appendix ends with extra qualitative comparisons and results for different noise degradation levels.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work, proofs, evaluation protocols, Gaussianity tests and extra qualitative results.
